Where it began

Shivnarine Chanderpaul was born on 16 August 1974 in Unity Village, Guyana, and it was his father who first nurtured his talent. By eight he was playing for the village team and batting for hours at a time while relatives took turns to bowl at him. At ten he was already turning out for a club's under-16 side.

He made his first-class debut for Guyana at seventeen, and in 1993 made an unbeaten double hundred for the West Indies Under-19 side at Trent Bridge. Within a year he was a Test cricketer.

The player

He made 62 in his first Test innings, against England in 1994, and finished his debut series with an average of 57.60. The first Test hundred took a while to arrive, coming against India in his nineteenth match, but after that they kept coming. Against Australia he and Ramnaresh Sarwan both made hundreds as the West Indies chased down 418 to win, something no Test side had done before, and he did it with a broken finger. On his first Test as captain he made 203 not out.

In 164 Tests from 1994 to 2015 he scored 11,867 runs at 51.37, with 30 hundreds, 66 fifties and a best of 203 not out.

What made him special

Nobody stood at the crease quite like him. He faced the bowler almost square-on, a habit from his boyhood that let him watch the ball with both eyes, then shuffled into position as it was bowled. It looked odd and worked beautifully. He also had a rare gift for not getting out: four times in his career he batted more than a thousand minutes in Tests between dismissals.

He began as an attacking player who took his nickname, Tiger, from Rohan Kanhai, one of his early influences, and became the steady anchor of the side. Shane Warne reckoned you needed a crowbar to shift him. They rarely found one.

Away from the middle

He was named one of Wisden's Cricketers of the Year and won the ICC Cricketer of the Year award in 2008. Guyana gave him the Cacique's Crown of Honour in 2009, the University of the West Indies made him an honorary Doctor of Laws in 2018, and he joined the ICC Hall of Fame in 2022. He played county cricket for Durham and Lancashire, and later coached the USA women's and Under-19 women's teams, taking the younger side to a World Cup in 2023.

And finally

The Jamaican singer Sean Paul once revealed that a line many fans thought was his own name being sung was in fact a shout for Chanderpaul, one of his sporting heroes. Plenty of batters have been cheered from the stands. Very few have been sung about without anyone noticing.
